newsitem.title: UK: UK Conservative leadership race nears climax.
newsitem.headline: UK Conservative leadership race nears climax.

text.p: Four of the five challengers for the leadership of Britain's defeated Conservative party trooped into the television studios on Sunday to set out their stall one last time before the first round of voting on Tuesday.

With the race still wide open, the contenders all portrayed themselves as best able to unite the party's feuding factions and rebuild grassroots support after the shattering loss to Tony Blair's Labour party in elections on May 1.

The name of the new leader, who will succeed former prime minister John Major, is impossible to predict because he will be chosen in a secret, complex ballot of the Conservatives' 164 remaining members of parliament.
Former finance minister Kenneth Clarke is favourite to win the first vote, but no one expects him to win outright.

For that, Clarke would have to win more than half the vote and be 15 percent ahead of the runner-up. But according to the Observer newspaper he can be sure of just 37 votes, while the Sunday Telegraph put the figure at 35.

Ex-Welsh Secretary William Hague, at 36 by far the youngest in the field, is tipped to come second on Tuesday with about 30 votes, followed by former interior minister Michael Howard and ex-social security secretary Peter Lilley.
John Redwood, the right-wing "Eurosceptic" who unsuccessfully challenged Major for the leadership two years ago, is expected to bring up the rear with about a dozen votes.
The contest will start in earnest after the first ballot when the trailing candidates must decide whether to run in the second round on June 17 or back one of the front-runners.
If there is no outright victor on June 17 -- when new contenders can join the race -- the two men who top the poll will fight it out in a third and final ballot on June 19.

Several newspaper commentators believe the Conservative best able to stand up to Blair, already the most popular prime minister on record with an approval rating of 82 percent, is Clarke, a richly experienced minister with a common touch.
Clarke highlighted his popular appeal on Sunday while playing down the pro-European views that make him anathema to Conservative Eurosceptics opposed to closer European ties.

"This leadership election is about a man. Has that man got strong enough political convictions, a clear enough vision of which way the party is going, enough wide broad, public appeal combined with the political ability to beat Tony Blair?" Clarke said on BBC television.

Hague, who critics say is untested and a younger version of the grey Major, said he had appeal right across the spectrum of Conservative opinion. "I think that puts me in a good position to unite the party after the election," he told GMTV.

Lilley, competent but short on charisma, predicted he would finish in the top three on Tuesday and would then expect the other two right-wingers, Howard and Redwood, to stand down and bring their supporters over to him.

"I am probably best placed because I am the candidate who comes broadly from the right of centre, who has the confidence of the right, but with an appeal across the whole spectrum of opinion in the party," Lilley told BBC television.
But Redwood, who has fought on a platform of fierce opposition to the planned European single currency, said he had no intention of dropping out of the second round of voting.
"I intend to carry on because I think the party has to make a decision (on Europe)," he told Sky television. REUTER
